"Arnab! Arnab!" Kalyani, six, was on the floor by the stool, clutching her knee, blood on her fingers.
Arnab, her big brother, dropped his pencil and knelt. His stomach flipped, but he kept his voice slow. "Okay. I see it. Don't touch it."
"It hurts!"
"I know. You're being brave. Stay here, I'm getting Ma."
He walked quickly, not running, to the kitchen. "Ma, Kalyani fell off the stool. Her knee's bleeding. Not a lot."
Ma turned off the gas. "Where's the first-aid box?"
"Top of the cupboard. I'll bring it."
When Ma knelt by Kalyani, Arnab was already there with the box open and a bandage in his hand.
"You stayed so calm," Ma said.
"My heart didn't," Arnab admitted.

First big accident on the highway: a boy trapped in a car, his mother screaming. I felt everything she felt. I shook so hard I dropped the kit. My senior, old Mathew sir, gripped my shoulder. 'Kishore. Breathe. Slowly. Now: what does this boy need from you?' I breathed. My hands steadied. I still cared, oh, I cared, but I wasn't drowning with her. After that shift he made me eat, sit in the sun, and sleep. 'A tired heart helps nobody,' he said. So I tell you the same. Breathe, ask what will help, then go home and rest.

Today I felt weird. I don't know how else to say it. At lunch Bhavna sat with the new girl instead of me, and my stomach went tight like a fist. Then my throat felt hot. Mummy asked at dinner, 'Are you angry? Sad?' I said, 'No, just weird.' She asked if I was jealous. I said no. I don't think I was. Or maybe a bit? 'Like before my board exams. Worried?' Parveen frowned. She didn't know. It didn't feel like a word, just a knot in her tummy. Ujjwal sat with her on the step. subtype: "I'm fine" while clearly not [Actor]
passage:
Monday. Vandana's best friend moved to Delhi. At dinner her mother, Madhuri, asked, 'How are you feeling, beta?' 'Fine.' Vandana went to bed at eight with a headache.
Thursday. 'Fine,' again, when her mother found her awake at one in the morning. 'My chest feels heavy. And my legs are tired.' Nothing about the friend.
The next Saturday. Madhuri sat on her bed with a sheet of paper listing feeling words. 'Just point, if any fit.' Vandana stared for a long time. Then, slowly, her finger went to lonely. Then to lost. She started to cry, and it felt, strangely, like relief.

qa.q: What did Madhuri bring on Saturday?
qa.a: A sheet of paper listing feeling words.

qa.q: Why did crying feel like relief to Vandana?
qa.a: Finally finding the words lonely and lost let Vandana understand the heaviness in her chest that had been there all week.

qa.q: Why was Madhuri's "Just point, if any fit" a good approach?
qa.a: It removed the pressure of explaining, letting Vandana recognise a feeling from a list instead of having to produce the words.

qa.q: What might the week have been like for Madhuri?
qa.a: Madhuri likely worried, hearing "fine" while seeing headaches and sleeplessness, and searched for a gentle way in.

grounding: Over a week, a teenager answers fine while describing aches, until her mother offers a list and she finds the words lonely and lost.

subtype: Partner feels shut out [Receiver]
passage: I'm Aditi, and for most of our first year together I thought Ishita didn't love me. When I cried after my grandmother's funeral, she held me but said nothing. When I asked, 'How do you feel about us?', she said, 'Good,' and changed the subject. I took it as coldness. I told my friends she was a wall. Then one night, after another 'good,' she went quiet and said, 'I don't know how to find the words. It's like everything's there, but in a language I can't read.' She'd been making my tea every morning for a year, exactly how I like it. I'd never counted that. Now I ask smaller questions, and I listen to what she does.

Sunday night

subtype: Learning words for feelings with support [Response]
passage: In the staff counselling room on the fifth floor, Kamal opened a small notebook and pushed it across the table. 'I did the homework.' Rukmini, the counsellor, smiled. Three weeks ago he had come in because his manager called him 'robotic' and his girlfriend, Neha, had said she felt alone with him. He'd said he had no idea what he felt, most days. Now the notebook held words for emotions, copied from a chart: irritated, disappointed, uneasy, proud. Each evening he had written one line. 'Tuesday: tight chest in the review meeting. Maybe… anxious?' 'Friday: warm when Neha laughed. Happy? Relieved?' Rukmini tapped the question marks. 'These are good. Guesses are how you learn.' Kamal almost smiled. qa.a: Guessing a feeling from a body cue is the very skill being built, so rewarding guesses keeps Kamal trying instead of fearing wrong answers.

qa.a: Neha, who felt alone, may start to feel closer as Kamal can name moments like feeling warm when she laughed.

passage:
Dear Keerthana,
You asked what I've been up to since I stopped answering 'how are you' with 'fine.' Here's the honest version.
In January my boss said I seemed 'checked out,' and I realised I couldn't even tell her what I was feeling. So I started small. I printed a page of emotion words and stuck it inside my wardrobe door. Every night I write two lines: what my body did today, and which word might fit. 'Jaw clenched on the bus: annoyed?' 'Heavy shoulders after Amma's call: guilty? tired?'
In March, when it still felt tangled, I booked a counsellor. Best decision.
So, to answer your question properly: today I feel hopeful. And a little shy telling you this.
Love,
Ayesha

subtype: Learning words for feelings with support [Response]
passage: Chetan, you remember how Pooja left last year saying I was 'impossible to reach'? I thought she was being dramatic. Honestly, I didn't know what she meant. Then my team lead said the same thing at work, and I thought, okay, Saurabh, maybe it's you. So I tried something. I found a feelings chart online, the kind they give kids, and started checking it every night. Where's my body tight? Chest? Neck? Then I'd guess a word. First month, every answer was 'stressed.'
